nameStory: The collared parachute gets its charming name from two distinctive features that make it unmistakable in the forest. Its tiny white cap looks just like a miniature parachute when viewed from above, complete with pleated 'fabric' radiating from the center. The 'collared' part comes from the unique way its gills attach to a distinctive collar or ring around the stem, rather than connecting directly to the stem itself.
description: The collared parachute is a delicate little mushroom that looks like nature's own tiny umbrella collection scattered through the woods. These petite fungi have thin, whitish caps up to about 3/4 inch wide that are deeply sunken in the center with pleated, scalloped edges that give them their parachute-like appearance. They sit atop remarkably thin, wiry black stems that can stretch up to 3 inches tall but are only about 1/16 inch thick. You'll typically find them growing in cheerful little clusters on rotting twigs, fallen branches, and moss-covered logs.

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: White gills that are widely spaced and attach to a distinctive collar around the stem rather than directly to the stem - this collar connection is unique and diagnostic

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Thin, membranous white cap deeply sunken in the center with pleated, scalloped margins that feel delicate and papery to the touch

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Remarkably slender, wiry black stem that's hollow and feels surprisingly tough despite being thread-thin

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows on decaying wood - look for them on fallen twigs, small branches, moss-covered logs, and old stumps

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Grows in small groups or clusters, often several mushrooms emerging from the same piece of rotting wood

habitat: Collared parachutes are common throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests, where they make their home on decaying hardwood debris. Look for them on fallen twigs, small branches, moss-covered logs, and old stumps in moist woodland areas from lowland forests to mid-elevation slopes. They're particularly fond of areas with consistent moisture and good leaf litter, thriving in the dappled shade of mature forest understories.

seasonality.spring: Early clusters may appear on winter debris as temperatures warm and spring rains provide moisture, typically starting in late April or May.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season when warm temperatures and summer showers create ideal conditions, with fresh clusters appearing regularly on rotting wood.
seasonality.fall: Continue fruiting actively through autumn as falling leaves create fresh habitat and consistent moisture, often persisting until hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: Mostly dormant, though dried specimens from fall may still be visible on logs and can actually revive and release spores when rewetted by winter thaws.

funFact: These tiny mushrooms are nature's ultimate survivors - when they dry out completely, they don't die but instead go into a kind of suspended animation, and when moisture returns, they can magically revive and continue releasing spores for up to three weeks, far longer than almost any other mushroom species!
confusionNotes: The collared parachute is most easily confused with other small Marasmius species, but the distinctive collar where the gills attach is your foolproof identifier - no other small white mushroom has this unique feature. Remember: 'Collar connection = collared parachute!' Other similar species either have gills that attach directly to the stem or grow on different substrates.
contextualKnowledge: This species is also called the 'pinwheel mushroom' because of its pleated, radiating cap pattern, and sometimes the 'horsehair fungus' due to its incredibly thin black stems. Despite having multiple common names, they all refer to the same distinctive little mushroom that's actually the type species for the entire Marasmius genus.
compareHints: Among its Marasmius relatives in New England, the collared parachute is distinguished by its unique gill-to-collar attachment and preference for small woody debris. The fairy ring marasmius grows in grass rather than on wood, while other parachute mushrooms like the rosy parachute have different colored stems or different gill arrangements. The bristled parachute is larger and grows on leaf litter rather than twigs and small branches.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Fairy ring marasmius stands out from other Marasmius species by its robust size and grassland habitat - most of its relatives are tiny and grow on dead wood or leaves.
Among its Marasmius relatives, Hair-stemmed Pinwheel is distinguished by being both the smallest and having the thinnest stems.
